description: Locally authored mathematical reference notes. Further-reading links are background resources, not claims of quoted or imported training data.

notes.title: Power and chain rules
notes.content: For real powers x^p, d(x^p)/dx=p*x^(p-1) wherever the real expression is differentiable. For composites use (f(g(x)))'=f'(g(x))*g'(x). Retain domain restrictions; division by a variable requires excluding zero.

notes.title: Product and quotient rules
notes.content: (uv)'=u'v+uv'. If v != 0, (u/v)'=(u'v-uv')/v^2. The derivative of a product is generally not the product of derivatives.

notes.title: Antiderivatives and constants
notes.content: An indefinite integral denotes a family F(x)+C on an interval where F'=f. Verify by differentiating. The real integral of 1/x is log|x|+C on intervals excluding zero, not an unrestricted log(x). Substitution requires the differential factor.

notes.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus
notes.content: If f is continuous on [a,b], F(x)=integral from a to x of f(t)dt is differentiable on (a,b) and F'=f. If G is an antiderivative, the definite integral is G(b)-G(a). Improper integrals require separate convergence checks.

notes.title: Mean value theorem
notes.content: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), a<b, some c in (a,b) satisfies f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a). Rolle's theorem adds f(a)=f(b). Continuity or differentiability cannot be silently omitted.

notes.title: Limits and one-sided behavior
notes.content: A finite two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree. The value at the point need not equal the limit. Infinity and undefined expressions are not interchangeable; 0/0 and infinity/infinity are indeterminate forms, not answers.

notes.title: Conditions for L’Hôpital’s rule
notes.content: For a 0/0 or infinity/infinity quotient, the derivative quotient limit can determine the original under the theorem's differentiability and nonvanishing denominator-derivative hypotheses. Do not apply the rule to a quotient that is not indeterminate. Other forms require a justified transformation.

notes.title: Taylor approximation and remainder
notes.content: A finite Taylor polynomial needs a remainder bound to justify numerical accuracy. If |f^(n+1)| <= M on the relevant interval, the Lagrange remainder is bounded by M*|x-a|^(n+1)/(n+1)!. A smooth function need not equal its Taylor series.

notes.title: Equation solving and extraneous roots
notes.content: For ax^2+bx+c=0 with a != 0, roots are (-b +/- sqrt(b^2-4ac))/(2a). Over the reals the discriminant must be nonnegative. Squaring, cancelling factors, or multiplying by a denominator can alter the solution set; substitute candidates into the original equation and respect excluded points.

notes.title: Absolute values and real domains
notes.content: For real x, sqrt(x^2)=|x|, not x without x>=0. Over complex numbers, principal roots and logarithms introduce branch restrictions. Cancelling a factor does not restore points excluded by the original denominator.

notes.title: Rank, nullity, and solving systems
notes.content: For A with n columns, rank(A)+nullity(A)=n. Ax=b is consistent iff rank(A)=rank([A|b]). A unique solution requires consistency and nullity zero. Parameter-dependent ranks may change at exceptional values.

notes.title: Invertibility and determinants
notes.content: A square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero, equivalently its rank equals its size. A proposed inverse B must satisfy AB=BA=I. For a 2 by 2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det=ad-bc, and the inverse is [[d,-b],[-c,a]]/(ad-bc) when the determinant is nonzero.

notes.title: Eigenvalues and diagonalization
notes.content: An eigenpair satisfies Av=lambda*v with v != 0. Eigenvalues solve det(A-lambda*I)=0. Algebraic multiplicity need not equal geometric multiplicity. A matrix is diagonalizable over the chosen field iff it has a basis of eigenvectors; distinct eigenvalues are sufficient, not necessary.

notes.title: Spectral theorem
notes.content: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis over the reals. A complex Hermitian matrix has the analogous unitary diagonalization. General real matrices need not have real eigenvalues or orthogonal eigenvectors.

notes.title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
notes.content: In an inner-product space, |<u,v>| <= ||u||*||v||. Equality holds iff u and v are linearly dependent, including the zero-vector cases. For complex spaces, use conjugate symmetry and a Hermitian inner product.

notes.title: Geometric series
notes.content: The infinite sum from n=0 of r^n is 1/(1-r) precisely when |r|<1. From n=1 it is r/(1-r). For |r|>=1 the usual infinite series diverges. The finite sum is (1-r^(N+1))/(1-r) for r != 1; at r=1 it is N+1.

notes.title: Convergence tests
notes.content: The p-series sum 1/n^p converges iff p>1. A ratio/root test value below one implies absolute convergence and above one implies divergence; equality to one is inconclusive. Terms tending to zero are necessary but not sufficient. Conditional convergence is not absolute convergence.

notes.title: Compactness and extrema
notes.content: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a set is compact iff it is closed and bounded. A continuous real function on a nonempty compact set attains its maximum and minimum. Closed and bounded does not characterize compactness in arbitrary metric or normed spaces.

notes.title: Continuity and differentiability
notes.content: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there; the converse fails, for example |x| at zero. Continuity on a compact metric domain implies uniform continuity. Pointwise continuity on an unbounded or noncompact set need not be uniform.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes
notes.content: P(A|B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B) requires P(B)>0. When P(A)>0 and P(B)>0, Bayes gives P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Independence must be justified, not assumed. Disjoint nonzero-probability events are not independent.

notes.title: Expectation and variance
notes.content: Expectation is linear whenever the relevant expectations exist; independence is not required. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y), assuming finite second moments. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance alone generally does not imply independence.

notes.title: First-order differential equations
notes.content: For y'+p(x)y=q(x), an integrating factor is exp(integral p(x)dx), on an interval where the coefficients satisfy the needed regularity. Check initial conditions and the interval of validity. Dividing by a factor involving y in a separable equation may lose equilibrium solutions.

notes.title: Groups and Lagrange’s theorem
notes.content: For a finite group G and subgroup H, |H| divides |G|. Consequently, the order of an element divides |G|. The converse claim that a subgroup exists for every divisor is false for general finite groups.

notes.title: Complex differentiability
notes.content: Cauchy–Riemann equations at a point alone do not guarantee complex differentiability there. Continuous first partial derivatives in a neighborhood together with the equations provide a sufficient condition. Holomorphic functions on an open set are analytic there.

notes.title: Residue theorem
notes.content: For a positively oriented simple closed contour and a function meromorphic inside and on it, with no poles on the contour, the integral equals 2*pi*i times the sum of enclosed residues. Account for winding numbers for more general contours; contour poles need separate treatment.

notes.title: Critical points and optimization
notes.content: At an interior differentiable local extremum the gradient is zero. A zero gradient alone does not guarantee an extremum. In one dimension a positive second derivative gives a strict local minimum and a negative one a strict local maximum; a zero second derivative is inconclusive. Check endpoints and constraints separately.

notes.title: Exact values and numerical error
notes.content: Keep exact fractions, radicals, and symbolic constants during derivations. Round only the final numerical value and state the precision. Numerical agreement at sample points is evidence, not a proof of a general identity. Distinguish truncation error from floating-point roundoff.
